clues: Accumulates in extravascular tissues when vascular permeability increases during acute inflammation.
Characterized by a specific gravity greater than 1.020 and abundant inflammatory cells.
Protein-rich extravascular fluid containing fibrinogen and leukocytes, unlike a transudate.
Generated from high-molecular-weight kininogen by the action of kallikrein.
Rapidly inactivated by angiotensin-converting enzyme (kininase II) in the lungs.
A vasoactive nonapeptide that causes arteriolar dilation, increased venular permeability, and pain.
Commonly caused by pyogenic bacteria such as Staphylococcus aureus.
Microscopically shows a central zone of liquefactive necrosis surrounded by preserved neutrophils.
A localized, walled-off collection of pus within a tissue or organ.
A focal pattern of chronic inflammation triggered by persistent intracellular microbes or foreign bodies.
Often contains multinucleated giant cells and a peripheral collar of T lymphocytes.
A microscopic aggregate of activated epithelioid macrophages attempting to wall off an offending agent.

terms.sub: Tissue Repair, Angiogenesis, and Wound Healing
clues: Appears pink, soft, and granular on the base of healing wounds 3 to 5 days after injury.
Not to be confused with granulomatous inflammation despite its similar name.
Specialized vascularized repair tissue composed of proliferating fibroblasts and newly formed capillaries.

terms.sub: Tissue Repair, Angiogenesis, and Wound Healing
clues: Crucial for wound contraction during healing by secondary intention.
Acquires cytoplasmic bundles of alpha-smooth muscle actin under the influence of TGF-beta.
A modified stromal cell combining features of a collagen-producing fibroblast and a contractile smooth muscle cell.
More common in individuals of African descent and frequently recurs after simple excision.
Histologically characterized by thick, glassy, eosinophilic collagen bundles.
An exuberant fibrous scar that grows beyond the boundaries of the original skin wound.
